message.content:
Lions (family **Felidae**) and zebras (family **Equidae**) belong to two different orders—Carnivora and Perissodactyla, respectively.  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the ancestor of the larger clade that contains both of those orders, namely the **Laurasiatheria**.  

In other words, the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, likely insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago during the late Cretaceous. This ancestor gave rise to the diverse lineages that eventually led to modern cats, horses, cows, bats, whales, and many other Laurasiatherian mammals.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want an answer. There's no tool needed. Just respond with the common ancestor. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be the last common ancestor of the family Felidae and Equidae. That is within the order Carnivora? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia; zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their last common ancestor would be at the level of the clade Eutheria (placental mammals), maybe earlier. But we can say they share a common ancestor at the level of the mammalian clade Eutheria, specifically the last common ancestor of the superorders Laurasiatheria. But more precisely, the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae would be the ancestor of the clade that includes both families, which is the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That clade is called the Laurasiatheria. So the common ancestor is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria. We can mention that it's a placental mammal from the late Cretaceous period.

Thus answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived around 70–80 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria. Or simply: The last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae is the ancestor of the Laurasiatherian clade. Provide context.
